title: A mind that rests on nothing (section 10)
word: A mind that rests on nothing
hook: a mind should arise that rests on nothing: the line said to have woken Huineng

segments.voice: Yesterday, no I have attained: Subhuti dwells in peace without the thought that he has. Your line: without I did.

A young man is selling firewood in a market town in southern China. He's poor, and the old account says he can't read. He delivers a load to a shop, and on the way out he hears a man reciting something. The words stop him where he stands. What is that? The Diamond Sutra, comes the answer. That's how the Platform Sutra, the book of this young man's life and teaching, tells it. His name is Huineng, and Chan and Zen remember him as a great ancestor. Later in the same account, one line of that sutra opens him all the way. It's today's.
screen: `A FIREWOOD SELLER.` → `A SUTRA HEARD IN PASSING.` → `HUINENG STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, a look back. The Buddha asks Subhuti: long ago, with the Buddha Dipankara, did the Tathagata receive any teaching? No, Subhuti says. Nothing was received. Second, adorning. Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-lands, make the worlds beautiful? No, because adorning is not adorning; that's why it's called adorning. It's the rhythm of the earlier sections. Third, the line. Therefore, the Buddha says, a bodhisattva should give rise to a pure mind like this: a mind that doesn't rest on sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts. A mind should arise that rests on nothing. Notice it doesn't say no mind should arise. The mind sees, hears, works. It just doesn't set up camp. A hand that catches a ball and lets it go is still a hand. Tradition says that later, when Huineng's teacher explained the sutra to him, it was at this line that he woke up completely. Fourth, the week. Giving without resting on anything. Not seen by marks. Even the raft. Nothing fixed. Four lines. No I have attained. Each was a place where the mind could have settled and made a home: the gift, the statue, the teaching, the prize, the credit. Each time, the sutra let it lift off again. Today's line names what was happening all week: the same mind, just not resting.
screen: `NOTHING RECEIVED FROM DIPANKARA.` · `ADORNING THAT ISN'T ADORNING.` · `A MIND THAT RESTS ON NOTHING.` · `A WEEK OF NOT SETTLING.` · then, large: `RESTING ON NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Let sounds come, a car, a fridge, your own breathing, and notice the mind land on one: that's a truck, that's too loud. Then let it lift, the way a bird lifts off a wire. You don't have to stop the landing; just catch one moment of lifting, and stay in the open space after it as long as it lasts.
A mind that rests on nothing. A mind that arises without resting on sights, sounds or thoughts: the line tradition says woke Huineng. Today's word.
screen: `A MIND THAT RESTS ON NOTHING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: resting on nothing. A bird on a wire, then open sky. That's the week, gathered up.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen this line is studied closely and often recited, and the story of Huineng hearing the Diamond Sutra is told in the Platform Sutra, a text read in those schools.

original.note: Sanskrit: not resting, not set down; the sutra's word for a mind that settles on nothing.

chat.says: Does a mind that rests on nothing mean you should stop thinking?
options: No: the mind still sees, hears and works; it just doesn't set up camp anywhere.
Yes: the sutra says no mind should arise at all, so stop every thought.
It means the mind should hold tight to this one line and nothing else.
chat.meaning: The sutra says a mind should arise that rests on nothing. It doesn't say no mind should arise; the mind works, without clinging.

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text. The section's closing image (a body like Mount Sumeru) is left out for length.

The Huineng story is given as the Platform Sutra's account and 'tradition says'; versions of the Platform Sutra differ on details (e.g. whether he awakened on first hearing, or fully on Hongren's later explanation of this line). Check the wording against the version the path uses.
'Can't read' follows the Platform Sutra's account of Huineng as unlettered; confirm.
Hook's 'southern China' follows the Platform Sutra's setting; confirm wording.
Original: apratishthita (Sanskrit text has apratishthitam cittam utpadayitavyam); confirm spelling.

Editor pass: the hook said one line stopped Huineng in the market and that this was today's line; in the Platform Sutra he is moved by the recitation in general and awakens fully at this line later, when Hongren explains the sutra. The hook now says that. The reciter was a man leaving the shop, not necessarily the customer, so 'a customer' became 'a man' (hook and myth). Cut 'You know this rhythm by now' (telling the listener what they know).
